body.p: Claims 2-26 are pending. Claims 2-6 and 26 have been amended. Claim 1 was previously cancelled, and no claims have been currently cancelled or added. No new matter has been added.
Applicant notes with appreciation the Examiner's acknowledgement of the Information Disclosure Statements filed October 13, 2021, August 26, 2022, and May 8, 2023.

The Examiner is thanked for the time and courtesy extended during the telephone interview of June 3, 2024. During the interview, a proposed amendment, similar to the one provided herein, to independent claim 2 was discussed. The Examiner agreed that the amendment appeared to overcome the rejection as written, and asked that some remarks be provided with regards to obviousness in view of the references. The interview then concluded.

Claims 2-26 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as allegedly being unpatentable over U.S. Patent Publication No. 2007/0299473 (Matos) in view of U.S. Patent Publication No. 2011/0018998 (Guzik). Applicant does not acquiesce to this rejection.
Independent claim 2 has been amended to clarify the claimed subject matter. For example, claim 2 recites:
A monitoring and defibrillation system for assisting a caregiver in treating a subject and acquiring images and video of the subject
during an emergency, the system comprising:
a video camera configured to acquire one or more still images and real-time video of the subject at a first framerate during
the emergency;

a data collection unit configured to collect data comprising at least ECG signals, SpO2 levels and blood pressure of the subject; a communications unit configured to establish a communication channel with a remote location; and
at least one processor communicatively coupled with the video camera, the data collection unit and the communications unit,
the at least one processor configured to:

establish at least one of cellular or wireless communication channel with the remote location, transmit the ECG signals, SpO2 levels and blood pressure of the subject to the remote location, transmit the acquired one or more still images of the subject to the remote location, determine, before transmitting the real-time video of the subject to the remote location, an available bandwidth of the communication channel, and in response to the available bandwidth exceeding a predetermined threshold bandwidth, transmit the real- time video of the subject to the remote location at the first framerate, and

p.u: onse to the available bandwidth not exceeding the predetermined threshold bandwidth, transmit the real-time video of the sub
ect to the remote location at a second framerate less than the first framerate.

body.p: As discussed during the Interview, neither Matos nor Guzik disclose or reasonably

suggest the claimed features. Guzik does not contemplate changing the framerate of video at all based on available bandwidth. Matos merely discloses that a user can manually adjust the framerate of a video that they are watching (Matos, [ 1710), but the framerate is not being adjusted automatically by a processor in response to the available bandwidth exceeding or not exceeding a predetermined threshold bandwidth.
Furthermore, it would not have been obvious to make the adjustment to the video

framerate automatically in response to the available bandwidth in view of Matos and Guzik. Although Matos recognizes that a user may want to adjust the framerate of a video, Matos clearly does not suggest that such an adjustment would or could be made by the processor "in response to the available bandwidth," as Matos only discloses that the user may adjust the framerate for his own video. There is no adjustment to the framerate being made without user intervention.

Guzik discloses assessing the bandwidth and determining whether the bandwidth is sufficient to support full-motion video. (Guzik, [0201]). But Guzik only contemplates one solution to dealing with the situation where the bandwidth does not support full motion video -

transmitting still shots (Id.) Accordingly, Guzik's solution to insufficient bandwidth is to send still shots - Guzik does not contemplate transmitting the video at a lower framerate in response to the bandwidth being too low.

When considered together, Guzik does not provide any suggestion that the framerate can or should be adjusted to the video in response to the available bandwidth. Matos contemplates that bandwidth limitations may affect the quality of the video, but the solution provided by Guzik is to transmit still images when the bandwidth is low, not to transmit video at a lower framerate. There is no reason a person of ordinary skill in the art would deviate from the teachings of Guzik in this regard.

For at least the reasons provided above, a prima facie case of obviousness cannot be established. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that the rejection of claim 2 be reconsidered and withdrawn. Also, dependent claims 3-26 should be found allowable, at least based on their dependence from claim 2, as well as for their additional distinguishing features.

Claims 5 and 6 stand rejected under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b) as allegedly being indefinite. Without acquiescing, Applicant has amended claims 3-6 to address any potential ambiguity. Accordingly, Applicant respectfully requests that this rejection be reconsidered and withdrawn.
